items.actClause:
AN ACT to amend the multiple dwelling law, in relation to occupancy of joint
living-work quarters for artists
items.memo:
BILL NUMBER: S8793

SPONSOR: KAVANAGH
 
TITLE OF BILL:

An act to amend the multiple dwelling law, in relation to occupancy of
joint living-work quarters for artists

 
PURPOSE:

To permit residents who live in joint live-work quarters for artists
(JLWQA) units and were in residence prior to December 31, 2021 to
continue occupying such unit regardless of their status as a certified
artist.

 
SUMMARY OF SPECIFIC PROVISIONS:

Section one adds a new subdivision 16 to section 277 of the multiple
dwelling law to permit residents who live in joint live-work quarters
for artists (JLWQA) units and were in residence prior to December 31,
2021 to continue occupying such unit regardless of their status as a "
certified artist.

Section 2 sets forth the effective date.

 
JUSTIFICATION:

For several decades, and preceding the Loft Law, residential use of
former manufacturing space has been permitted in SoHo and NoHo as Joint
Live-Work Quarters for Artists (JLWQA) under Article 7-B of the Multiple
Dwelling Law. Residential use of space zoned for commercial use was
permitted in order to preserve housing and to support artists who used
their lofts as live-work space and greatly contributed to the character
of their neighborhoods.

In late 2021, a zoning change was adopted for SoHo and NoHo that allowed
buildings currently zoned for commercial use to be rezoned for residen-
tial use despite the many non-conforming activities that artists who
occupy live-work spaces may engage in. It appears that the City's
enforcement of the certified artist requirement for occupancy of these
units before the 2021 rezoning had been minimal for many years. Many
long-standing residents of JLWQA units that had not successfully
completed the certification through the NYC Department of Cultural
Affairs were not offered a feasible path toward obtaining this certif-
ication, leaving them vulnerable to fines and undermining their right to
occupy their homes. There are several reasons why a resident may lack
certification as an artist, including overly stringent City requirements
for what constitutes "fine art," lack of responsiveness from DCA, and
ongoing occupancy of a family home by a non-certified artist after a
family member who was a certified artist has died.

Local elected officials are considering adjustments to the certification
process. In the meantime, this legislation will ensure that long-term
residents of the community who may lack artist certification for whatev-
er reason are not displaced from their homes.

 
LEGISLATIVE HISTORY:

New bill.
 
FISCAL IMPLICATIONS:

None.

 
EFFECTIVE DATE:
This act shall take effect immediately.

BILL NUMBER: S8793A   Revised 5/17/22

SPONSOR: KAVANAGH
 
TITLE OF BILL:

An act to amend the multiple dwelling law, in relation to occupancy of
joint living-work quarters for artists

 
PURPOSE:

To permit residents who live in joint live-work quarters for artists
(JLWQA) units and were in residence prior to December 15, 2021 to
continue occupying such unit regardless of their status as a certified
artist.

 
SUMMARY OF SPECIFIC PROVISIONS:

Section 1 adds a new sentence to section 276 of the multiple dwelling
law to permit residents who live in joint live-work quarters for artists
(JLWQA) units and were in residence prior to December 15, 2021 to
continue occupying such unit regardless of their status as a certified
artist.

Section 2 sets forth the effective date.

 
JUSTIFICATION:

For several decades, and preceding the Loft Law, residential use of
former manufacturing space has been permitted in SoHo and NoHo as Joint
Live-Work Quarters for Artists (JLWQA) under Article 7-B of the Multiple
Dwelling Law. Residential use of space zoned for commercial use was
permitted in order to preserve housing and to support artists who used
their lofts as live-work space and greatly contributed to the character
of their neighborhoods.

In late 2021, a zoning change was adopted for SoHo and NoHo that allowed
buildings currently zoned for commercial use to be rezoned for residen-
tial use despite the many non-conforming uses in which artists and non-
artists occupy live-work spaces. It appears that the City's enforcement
of the certified artist requirement for occupancy of these units before
the 2021 rezoning had been minimal for many years. Many long-standing
residents of JLWQA units that had not successfully completed the certif-
ication through the NYC Department of Cultural Affairs were not offered
a feasible path toward obtaining this certification, leaving them
vulnerable to fines and undermining their right to occupy their homes.
There are several reasons why a resident may lack certification as an
artist, including overly stringent City requirements for what consti-
tutes "fine art," lack of responsiveness from DCLA, and ongoing occupan-
cy of a family home by a non-certified artist after a family member who
was a certified artist has died.

Local elected officials are considering adjustments to the certification
process. In the meantime, this legislation will ensure that long-term
residents of the community who may lack artist certification for whatev-
er reason are not displaced from their homes.

 
LEGISLATIVE HISTORY:

New bill.
 
FISCAL IMPLICATIONS:

None.

 
EFFECTIVE DATE:
This act shall take effect immediately.
